data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which of the following is NOT a barrier to mukti?
data.targetWord: Wisdom

examples.en-GB: Answer: Wisdom | Distractors: Anger; Greed; Illusion

data.sourceWord: Sewa — physical and material service
data.targetWord: Sikhs carry out sewa through tan (physical service such as cleaning the gurdwara or serving langar) and dhan (material service such as donating food or paying daswandh).

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — ways Sikhs carry out sewa

data.sourceWord: Sewa — mental service and community support
data.targetWord: Man sewa (mental service) includes teaching others to read the Guru Granth Sahib, supporting worshippers, or gaining a deeper understanding of faith to serve the spiritual community.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — ways Sikhs carry out sewa

data.sourceWord: Women's equality — equal roles in the gurdwara
data.targetWord: Sikh belief in the equality of women means they may serve as granthi (reader), ragi (musician), or prepare karah parshad — all key gurdwara roles based entirely on character and ability, not gender.

data.sourceWord: Women's equality — Khalsa membership and leadership
data.targetWord: Women have an equal right to join the Khalsa, take amrit, and follow the Rehit Maryada. Guru Gobind Singh's wife was in the Khalsa and led it after his death; women can also be warriors.

data.sourceWord: Haumai — barrier to mukti
data.targetWord: Haumai (ego/pride) is one of the Five Evils all Sikhs must eradicate. It makes a person manmukh (self-centred) rather than gurmukh (God-centred), preventing spiritual progress and mukti.

data.sourceWord: Haumai — selfishness opposes sewa
data.targetWord: Pride makes a person selfish, which directly contradicts Sikhism's core teaching of selfless service (sewa). By eliminating haumai, a Sikh can fulfil their duties and move closer to gurmukh.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: haumai in the Guru Granth Sahib
data.targetWord: 'Those who do not serve the true Guru…they go through 8.4 million reincarnations, and they are ruined by death and rebirth.' (Guru Granth Sahib) — showing the consequence of remaining in haumai.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Sangat is the school of the soul
data.targetWord: 'The Sat Sangat is the school of the soul, where the Glorious Virtues of the Lord are studied.' (GGS) — the Sangat provides spiritual support, teaching, and community that enables Sikhs to progress.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Gurus set up and commended the Sangat
data.targetWord: The Sangat dates back to Guru Nanak himself. The Gurus taught it was best for all and set it up for the spiritual development of the community, making it uniquely authoritative for Sikhs.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: The Sangat organises sewa — service is more important
data.targetWord: The Sangat's most important role may be organising sewa, ensuring the langar runs and the community is served. The practical acts of service may matter more than the spiritual community itself.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Not all Sikhs can access the Sangat
data.targetWord: Not all Sikhs live near a physical Sangat, and not all practising Sikhs choose to belong to one. This limits its claim to be the most important aspect of Sikh spirituality for everyone.

data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which structure houses the Guru Granth Sahib?
data.targetWord: A domed structure for the Guru Granth Sahib

examples.en-GB: Answer: A domed structure for the Guru Granth Sahib | Distractors: A place of meditation; A cooking hall; A community centre

data.sourceWord: Langar — equality in practice
data.targetWord: The langar (free community kitchen) is prepared, cooked and served equally by men and women. All eat together on the floor without hierarchy, embodying the Sikh belief in the equality of all people.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — importance of the langar

data.sourceWord: Langar — sewa and feeding the community
data.targetWord: Serving in the langar is an act of sewa (selfless service). It provides free food to all visitors regardless of background, demonstrating Sikh values of generosity and care for the wider community.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q2.2 — importance of the langar

data.sourceWord: Amrit ceremony — initiation into the Khalsa
data.targetWord: The Amrit ceremony (Amrit Sanskar) initiates Sikhs into the Khalsa. Amrit (sweetened water stirred with a khanda) is shared; the initiate commits to following the Rehit Maryada and wearing the 5 Ks.

data.sourceWord: Amrit ceremony — transformation and community
data.targetWord: After taking amrit, men take the name Singh (lion) and women take Kaur (princess), symbolising equality and courage. The ceremony strengthens identity as part of the Khalsa community.

data.sourceWord: Vaisakhi — Khalsa foundation and celebration
data.targetWord: Vaisakhi (April 13) commemorates the founding of the Khalsa by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699. It is celebrated with prayers, processions (nagar kirtan), and amrit ceremonies for new Khalsa members.

data.sourceWord: Vaisakhi — harvest festival and Sikh identity
data.targetWord: Vaisakhi also marks the Punjabi harvest festival and is one of the most important dates for Sikhs to affirm their identity and commitment to the Khalsa ideals of service, equality and justice.

data.sourceWord: Scripture: Sikh equality from the Adi Granth
data.targetWord: 'Women and men, all by God are created. All this is God's play. Says Nanak, all thy creation is good.' (Guru Granth Sahib) — affirming the equal status of all people before God.

data.sourceWord: FOR: Vaisakhi is most important — founding of the Khalsa
data.targetWord: Vaisakhi commemorates the founding of the Khalsa in 1699 — the defining moment in Sikh history. Without the Khalsa, much of Sikh identity, practice and community would not exist.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Diwali (Bandi Chhor Divas) is more important for some
data.targetWord: Sikhs celebrate Diwali as Bandi Chhor Divas — the day Guru Hargobind was freed from prison. For many Sikhs this represents justice and liberation, values equally central to their faith.

data.answer: Haumai means ego or pride which is a barrier to mukti.
Sewa means selfless service in the Sikh community.
The langar provides free food for all regardless of background.

data.title: The Five Ks (Panj Kakars) in Sikhism
data.sourceTitle: The Five Ks (Panj Kakars) in Sikhism
data.sourcePassage: The Five Ks (Panj Kakars) are five articles of faith that initiated Sikhs (members of the Khalsa) wear at all times. They were established by Guru Gobind Singh at the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Kesh (uncut hair) represents respect for God's creation and is covered by a dastar (turban). Kangha (a small comb) symbolises cleanliness and order. Kara (a steel bracelet) represents infinity, strength and the bond with God. Kachera (cotton undergarment) symbolises self-control and modesty. Kirpan (a small sword) represents justice, courage and the duty to defend the weak. Together, the Five Ks mark a Sikh as a member of the Khalsa, demonstrate commitment to Sikh values, and provide a visible identity in the world. The Khalsa was created to stand up for righteousness (dharam) and protect the oppressed, and the Five Ks are a daily reminder of this calling.
